_about: Genre configurations for Spectre. One entry per genre; `studio.py master --genre <name>` takes the target curve and the mastering settings from `master` (explicit flags override). Every value names its source in the genre doc (`doc`) or below; `hand_tuned` lists values that have no published source yet. There is no default genre.

trap.name: Trap / beats (808-driven: trap, boom-bap, drill, rage, folk-fusion trap)
trap.status: the configuration of the first releases of sessions 001-006, preserved exactly (the former engine default; `--target beat` is an alias; add `--legacy-master` to reproduce those masters). Sessions 001-006 were remastered with `hiphop` on 2026-11-24
trap.form: an intro, a real arrangement (hooks and verses) and an outro
trap.tempo: 130-160 bpm with a half-time feel (65-80 felt); sessions 001-006 ran 136-160
trap.role: it should feel like a real beat an artist could rap on
hand_tuned: target curve `beat` (808 sub-forward; not measured from references)
translate 0.5
eq 0.7
sources: length: Billboard Hot 100 top-10 hip-hop hits averaged 2:48 in 2019 (Billboard, https://www.billboard.com/?p=8514407, not re-verified 2026-11: page unreachable); Spotify charting songs averaged about 3:00 in 2024, hip-hop -29 s since 2018 (Chartmetric, https://hmc.chartmetric.com/shorter-songs-trend-streaming-history/)
tempo: Mixgraph genre index lists trap (hip-hop) at 130-150 bpm, half-time feel ~70 (https://www.mixgraph.io/bpm-for)

loudness: 54 Billboard Global 200 top-10 songs (H1 2024) averaged -8.3 LUFS integrated, sd 1 LU (iZotope, https://www.izotope.com/en/learn/mastering-trends); -10.5 is an engine-limited choice (the true-peak guard stops gaining past about -9.5), streaming normalizes to -14 (Spotify)

hiphop.name: Hip-hop / trap with a measured tonal target (researched alternative to `trap`)
hiphop.status: same as `trap` except the tonal target, which is the measured hip-hop spectrum; the configuration for beat sessions (sessions 001-006 remastered with it, master version 2, 2026-11-24)
hiphop.form: intro 4, verse 16, hook 8, verse 16, hook 8, (bridge 8), outro 4; about 60-72 bars (felt bars at half-time tempos)
hiphop.tempo: two pockets: boom-bap / hardcore 85-100 bpm, swung 16ths; trap-leaning 130-150 bpm written, felt in half time (~70)
hiphop.meter: 4/4; backbeat on 2 and 4 (on 3 in half-time trap)
hiphop.change_rate: something changes every 4-8 bars; sections of 8 or 16 bars (verse 16, hook 8)
hiphop.role: it should feel like a real beat an artist could rap on
hand_tuned: translate 0.5
eq 0.7
change_rate (craft, docs/CRAFT.md)
lufs -10.5 is an engine-limited choice, quieter than the charts (-8.3); a louder hiphop master is an open test
sources: target curve: hip-hop average spectrum, Pestana, Ma, Reiss, Barbosa & Black (2013), AES 135th Convention, Fig. 5, converted to 1/3-octave bands (see docs/MASTERING.md)
everything else: as `trap`
tempo, form, loudness, width, role (researched 2026-11-24): docs/HIPHOP.md, section Configuration (Mixgraph hip-hop and trap tempo data, Berklee Today, eMastered, iZotope 2024, Soundfly, Splice)

trance.name: Trance (uplifting, progressive, euphoric), extended mix
trance.length: 6:00-8:00 (extended mix); a radio edit (`trance_radio`, measured median 3:33) only on request
trance.form: DJ intro 16-32 bars, theme 16-32, build 8-16, first drop 16-32, breakdown 16-64 (typically 32), build 8-16, main drop 32-64, DJ outro 16-32
trance.change_rate: add or remove an element every 4, 8, 16 or 32 bars; work in 16-bar blocks
trance.role: a lead synth carries the melody a vocalist would sing; DJ-mixable intro and outro
hand_tuned: translate 0.4
eq 0.7
lufs -10 is an engine-limited choice, quieter than the charts (-8.3)
trance.sources: docs/TRANCE.md, section Configuration Mastering loudness: docs/proposals/mastering-trance-poprock.md (dance/electronic chart top 10 2025 average -8.3 LUFS, rock/alternative 2025 average -8.1, iZotope; engine tests: trance clipper limits it to about -9, rock clean at -8.5).

trance_radio.name: Trance, radio edit (the short cut of a trance single: no DJ intro or outro, one breakdown, two drops)
trance_radio.status: researched 2026-11-24 for session 013; everything not listed here is as `trance` (tempo, meter, groove, sound); the master is the `trance` master unchanged (measured: radio edits are as loud as their long versions)
trance_radio.length: 3:00-4:00, aim 3:15-3:50 (measured median 3:33, middle half 3:15-3:49, 1,072 trance radio edits); at 138 bpm about 112-132 bars
trance_radio.form: intro 8 bars (the track identifiable within 5-15 s, no DJ drums), theme 8-16, build 8, first drop 16 (landing at about 0:40-1:05), breakdown 16 (24 at most), build 8, main drop 32, outro 4-16 (a hard end or a short tail, no DJ outro); two drops around one breakdown; about 120 bars = 3:29 at 138 bpm
trance_radio.change_rate: something every 8-16 bars, blocks of 8 more often than in the extended mix; 32 bars (the main drop) at most
trance_radio.role: a lead synth carries the melody a vocalist would sing; no DJ intro or outro needed: the track must say what it is in the first seconds
hand_tuned: translate 0.4
eq 0.7
lufs -10 is an engine-limited choice, quieter than the charts (-8.3)
the section lengths are derived (measured total length and paired cut, arithmetic over the extended template), not measured bar by bar
first-drop position: derived, no trance measurement found
sources: length: MusicBrainz, recordings tagged trance titled 'radio edit', grouped by artist and title: 1,072 tracks, median 3:33, middle half 3:15-3:49, 10th-90th 2:59-4:04; 177 pairs with an extended or original mix: radio 3:30 vs 6:39, 52% kept, 3:07 cut (Spectre's count 2026-11-24, docs/TRANCE.md); all club genres: radio edits median 3:30 over 803 titles (https://www.mixgraph.io/glossary/radio-edit)

form: DJ ends removed and a hard ending (https://www.mixgraph.io/glossary/radio-edit), intro build-ups removed or halved (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_edit), no two-minute breakdowns on the radio (Bill Padley, https://www.soundonsound.com/people/bill-padley-wise-buddamusic-ltd-music-production-recording-editing-radio-tv), intro 5-10 s (https://waterbear.org.uk/blog/how-to-make-a-radio-edit-for-radio-play/), builds doubling every 1-2 bars and 1-2 bar gaps (https://www.musicradar.com/how-to/8-classic-recipes-for-a-perfect-drop)
master: 70 radio/long pairs with AcousticBrainz ReplayGain: radio edit median 0.0 dB louder (middle half -1.1 to +1.1), so the `trance` master is kept; its own sources in docs/TRANCE.md, Mastering

rock.name: Pop rock (band song form)
rock.form: intro (about 4-8 bars), verse, pre-chorus, chorus, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, final chorus (often doubled), outro; sections of 8 bars (4 and 16 common); first chorus by about 0:45-0:60
rock.tempo: 115-130 bpm typical (partly sourced; ballad builders start slower)
rock.change_rate: every section (8 bars); dynamics between sections are the main tool
rock.role: the verses leave room for a voice; a vocal-like lead carries the sung melody
hand_tuned: translate 0.3
eq 0.7
lufs -10 is an engine-limited choice, quieter than the charts (-8.1)
meter (no source sought: genre definition)
rock.sources: docs/POP_ROCK.md, section Configuration Mastering loudness: docs/proposals/mastering-trance-poprock.md (dance/electronic chart top 10 2025 average -8.3 LUFS, rock/alternative 2025 average -8.1, iZotope; engine tests: trance clipper limits it to about -9, rock clean at -8.5).

joc.name: Joc țigănesc: Romanian lăutar wedding dance music (solo violin, guitar, bass, percussion)
joc.status: researched 2026-11-24; the tonal target reuses the measured `rock` curve until the folk curve of Pestana et al. 2013 (Fig. 5) can be extracted
joc.form: rounds of a dance tune: strains of 8 or 16 bars of 2/4, each repeated with variation, faster each round; an optional slow (rar) opening, then the fast (repede) dance, an accelerating last round and a stop; primas preludes and interludes
joc.tempo: dance tempo quarter = 110-140 in 2/4; a slow rar or listening section can sit far lower (the reference score's practice ladder runs 50, 70, 90, 110); tempo rises round by round and accelerates at the end (section bpm ramps)
joc.meter: 2/4: bass on the beats, chords on the afterbeats; one engine pattern bar = two bars of 2/4
joc.change_rate: something changes every strain (8-16 bars of 2/4 = 4-8 pattern bars); the tempo steps up each round
joc.role: the violin leads throughout (melody, preludes, interludes, improvisation); guitar and bass hold the afterbeat (tiitura); percussion carries the dancers; a voice is optional (shouts to the dancers)
hand_tuned: target curve: `rock` reused (not measured on folk or lautar records)
lufs -11: a choice inside the sourced folk range of -14 to -10
translate 0.3
eq 0.7
change_rate (derived from the dance form; the exact rate is craft)
sources: length: seven Taraf de Haidouks recordings on AcousticBrainz, 2:51-7:14, median 5:21 (docs/JOC_TIGANESC.md, Sources)

form and tempo: the reference score's four passes at quarter = 50/70/90/110; Dans Tiganesc Rar (6/8) then Repede (2/4) (https://socalfolkdance.org/dances/D/Dans_Tiganesc_Rar-Dans_Tignanesc_Repede.pdf); slow-medium-fast-faster order and accelerations (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gypsy_style); AcousticBrainz tempo estimates 94-172 bpm

role: the primas leads (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_folk_violin); a wedding band with violin, guitar, string bass, accordions, cimbalom and a vocalist (Beissinger 2007, https://journals.ku.edu/folklorica/article/view/3757)
loudness: folk masters -14 to -10 LUFS, LRA at least 6 LU (https://www.sageaudio.com/articles/mastering-for-folk-music); acoustic genres near -16 (RoEx, advice); chart average -8.3 (iZotope 2024)

tonal balance: acoustic genres show a natural top-end decay; folk has the lowest spectral centroid, 603 Hz (Pestana et al. 2013); `rock` is the measured curve with the steepest top of the three available

caroling.name: American Christmas caroling: a carolers' choir (upper voices), handbells, brass, organ, strings; acoustic, no drum kit
caroling.status: researched 2026-11-24 for session 012; the tonal target reuses the measured `rock` curve (no choral or folk curve is measured yet), loudness from the Billboard Holiday 100 measurements (iZotope 2025) and a catalogue estimate of choral and a cappella Christmas albums (AcousticBrainz)
caroling.length: 2:00-3:30, typically 2:20-3:15 (one carol, a few verses; medleys and concert anthems run longer)
caroling.form: strophic: verses of 4 or 8 phrases (each 2 or 4 bars) with a refrain or chorus; 2-4 verses; variation by texture between verses (unison, harmony, a descant, a key lift, a bells or brass interlude), an intro of the last phrase or a bell peal, a held or ritardando ending
caroling.tempo: felt pulse about 50-60 per dotted quarter in 6/8 carols, quarter = 84-112 in duple and triple carols; slow carols lower; rubato and a final ritardando
caroling.meter: 3/4, 6/8 or 4/4; no backbeat; a 3-beat carol bar = 12 steps (4 carol bars = 3 engine bars)
caroling.change_rate: by verse and phrase: something changes every verse (4-8 carol bars), dynamics and texture inside a verse follow the words
caroling.role: the carolers carry the tune as a choir texture (voices as instruments: wordless or short refrain fragments, a call at the door); bells, brass and organ answer and fill; no lead vocal carrying verses
hand_tuned: target curve: `rock` reused (the steepest measured top; not measured on choral or acoustic Christmas records)
lufs -14: a choice between the Holiday 100 average (-12.9) and choral albums (about -19 to -23, estimated)
eq 0.5: lighter than other genres because the curve is not measured on this music
translate 0.2: little bass-harmonic enhancement (no bass instrument leads)
change_rate (craft, from the strophic form)
sources: length: MusicBrainz track lengths of five Christmas choral and a cappella albums (Ray Conniff Singers, Here We Come A-Caroling, 1965: median 2:25; Pentatonix 2014: 3:05; Straight No Chaser 2008: 3:13; Chanticleer 2010: 2:39; King's College 1986: 3:10), docs/CAROLING.md

loudness: Billboard Holiday 100 (week of 6 Dec 2025), 10 songs: average -12.9 LUFS integrated, range -8.8 to -23.3, LRA 7.0 LU (https://www.izotope.com/community/blog/holiday-songs-lufs-2025); AcousticBrainz ReplayGain of the albums above, calibrated on Spectre's own masters (LUFS = -23.7 - RG, about +-1 dB): a cappella pop about -12 to -14, choral and caroling albums about -19 to -23 (docs/CAROLING.md)
form and tempo: hymnal settings (Hutchins, Carols Old and Carols New, Boston 1916; Bramley & Stainer 1871), Mutopia MIDI tempo marks, AcousticBrainz tempo estimates (docs/CAROLING.md)
tonal balance: acoustic genres show a natural top-end decay (Pestana et al. 2013); docs/MASTERING.md

latinpop.name: Latin pop, intimate strands: bachata, bolero / romantic ballad, Latin pop ballad, Latin acoustic pop, soft reggaeton-pop (romantic dembow)
latinpop.status: researched 2026-11-24 for session 014; tempo, length and loudness measured on a catalogue of 25 albums (MusicBrainz lengths, AcousticBrainz tempo and ReplayGain) plus Mixgraph's reggaeton data; the tonal target reuses the measured `rock` curve (the mean of Pestana et al.'s pop and rock: the closest measured curve; no Latin curve is measured)
latinpop.length: 3:00-4:00, typically 3:15-3:50 (catalogue median 3:41 for releases since 2010, middle half 3:12-3:59; by strand: reggaeton-pop 3:21, bolero 3:35, bachata 3:59)
latinpop.form: song form in 8-bar sections: intro 4-8 (often the lead guitar or piano alone), verse, chorus, verse, chorus, a bridge or instrumental break, final chorus, outro; bachata maps it to its rhythm sections: derecho in the verses, majao in the choruses, mambo in the bridge or interlude (the most energetic part, where the singer stops and the guitars and bongos solo)
latinpop.tempo: by strand (catalogue medians, middle half): bachata 128 (122-133); bolero 82 (77-92; 60-90 typical); Latin pop ballad and acoustic pop about 75-80 (66-105, tempo octave ambiguous); reggaeton-pop 96 (91-114), reggaeton 95 (90-98, Mixgraph, 317 tracks)
latinpop.meter: 4/4 (Cuban boleros are often written in 2/4); straight 8ths in bachata and bolero, 16ths with light swing in dembow
latinpop.change_rate: by section (8 bars); in bachata the percussion changes with the section (derecho to majao at the chorus, mambo in the break); arrangements grow by adding the second guitar, bass, percussion, strings
latinpop.role: the instrumental carries the melody a singer would sing: requinto or nylon guitar, piano or a voice used as an instrument (a refrain fragment, a call); the accompaniment leaves the middle for it
hand_tuned: target curve: `rock` reused (pop+rock #1s 1950-2010; not measured on Latin records)
lufs -11: a choice inside the measured range (bolero about -13, bachata since 2010 -9.7, ballads -10.2, reggaeton-pop -10.6, chart average -8.3); intimate strands sit at the quieter end
eq 0.6: lighter than pop/rock because the curve is borrowed and acoustic arrangements have less 100-400 Hz body
translate 0.3 (a bass guitar or bass line is present in most strands)
change_rate (craft)
sources: length, tempo, keys, loudness: Spectre's catalogue of 25 albums (2026-11-24): MusicBrainz track lengths, AcousticBrainz (Essentia) tempo estimates (octave-folded per strand) and ReplayGain (LUFS ~ -23.7 - RG, calibrated on Spectre's masters, docs/CAROLING.md); album list and numbers in docs/LATIN_POP.md

reggaeton tempo: median 95 bpm, middle half 90-98, 317 tracks (https://www.mixgraph.io/bpm-for/reggaeton); 85-100 typical (https://www.musicradar.com/news/beat-building-how-to-produce-a-reggaeton-beat)
bolero tempo 60-90 bpm (https://www.soundbrenner.com/blogs/articles/bolero-rhythm)

bachata sections derecho / majao / mambo and instrument roles (https://ubisoft.com/en-au/game/rocksmith/plus/news-updates/4JGuRsatSHe2lZ4XuGxuUF/breaking-down-bachata-part-1-overview; part 2 percussion, part 3 guitars)

loudness: Latin masters -14 to -8 LUFS, about -12 to keep dynamics, traditional styles -16 to -12, hip-hop-leaning louder (https://sageaudio.com/articles/mastering-for-latin-music); chart top 10 average -8.3 LUFS (https://www.izotope.com/en/learn/mastering-trends)
tonal balance: Pestana et al. 2013 (docs/MASTERING.md)

chamberscore.name: Cinematic chamber score, whimsical and nostalgic (the childhood-montage idiom of animation and indie-film scores: piano, small strings with pizzicato, glockenspiel, celesta, vibraphone, woodwinds, acoustic guitar, ukulele, whistling, one orchestral swell), blended with neo-classical piano
chamberscore.status: researched 2026-11-24 for session 015; length, tempo estimates, keys and loudness measured on a catalogue of 30 albums (16 film and animation scores, 9 neo-classical, 5 indie-folk / chamber; MusicBrainz lengths, AcousticBrainz tempo, key and ReplayGain); form, meter and tempo of reference cues from analyses (Married Life: Hooktheory and an AAU thesis); the tonal target reuses the measured `rock` curve with a light EQ (no orchestral or acoustic curve is measured)
chamberscore.length: 3:00-4:30, aim 3:15-4:10 (a standalone track built like a montage cue: Married Life 4:11; score cues of 2:00 and longer median 2:52, middle half 2:18-3:32; standalone neo-classical and indie-folk tracks median 4:17 and 3:42)
chamberscore.form: theme and variations on one motif: 16-bar periods (A, A', B; Married Life is two AABA cycles with an intro, a break and a closing period), the theme passed between instruments and recoloured; joy and sorrow from the SAME theme by tempo, density and dynamics (a ritardando and a thinning to piano alone), not by switching to minor; one orchestral swell; the return of the theme changed; a slow piano close (Married Life falls from about 175 to 75 bpm); a late whole-tone lift is a habit of the idiom to question
chamberscore.tempo: two pockets: a waltz felt in one, quarter about 150-180 (dotted half 50-60: Married Life 172-175, Merry-Go-Round of Life chorus 161); piano-led cues in 4/4 or 2/4 about 72-104 (Spirited Away 77, Path of the Wind 90, Comptine 100, River Flows in You 72); the slow close about 70-80; rubato and ritardandi at phrase ends
chamberscore.meter: 3/4 (a waltz, felt in one: 12 engine steps per bar, 4 waltz bars = 3 engine bars) or 4/4 / 2/4; no drum kit (brushes, a light shaker or claps at most)
chamberscore.change_rate: by phrase and period: something changes every 8-16 bars (the theme moves to another instrument, a layer joins or leaves); the big changes are tempo, density and dynamics
chamberscore.role: a piano or a whimsical lead (glockenspiel, celesta, whistle, violin, clarinet-like reed) carries the theme; the accompaniment (waltz bass and chords, pizzicato, guitar or ukulele strums) leaves the middle for it; a voice, if any, is an instrument (a wordless line, a hum, a children's-choir colour)
hand_tuned: target curve: `rock` reused (pop+rock #1s 1950-2010; not measured on scores, piano or chamber music; the steepest measured top)
lufs -15: a choice between the score albums since 2005 (median -14.9) and neo-classical since 2005 (-16.7), inside Sage Audio's film range at its quiet edge
eq 0.4: lighter than caroling (0.5) because the curve is borrowed and a chamber ensemble has little 100-400 Hz body to match it
translate 0.2: little bass-harmonic enhancement (no bass instrument leads)
mono_below 80: lower than the band genres (Sage Audio: keep the low end of the side image in classical masters); the exact value is a choice
change_rate (craft, from the period form)
sources: length, tempo estimates, keys, loudness: Spectre's catalogue of 30 albums (2026-11-24): MusicBrainz track lengths, AcousticBrainz tempo, key and ReplayGain (LUFS ~ -23.7 - RG, calibrated on Spectre's masters, docs/CAROLING.md); album list and numbers in docs/CHAMBER_SCORE.md

form, meter, tempo of Married Life (Up): Hooktheory (F major, 3/4, 174 bpm, https://www.hooktheory.com/theorytab/view/michael-giacchino/up---married-life); AAU master's thesis on Married Life (16-bar A/A'/B variants, two AABA cycles, 175 to 75 bpm, sorrow by tempo, dynamics and solo piano in a major key, F to G lift; https://projekter.aau.dk/projekter/files/281254258/)

tempo and meter of reference cues: Hooktheory (Merry-Go-Round of Life 3/4 110/161; Spirited Away main theme 4/4 77; Path of the Wind 4/4 90; Comptine d'un autre ete 4/4 100; River Flows in You 2/4 72)

loudness: film and TV music -14 to -10 LUFS (https://www.sageaudio.com/articles/mastering-music-for-film-and-video); dynamic classical -20 to -16 LUFS, keep the low side image (https://sageaudio.com/articles/how-to-master-dynamic-classical-music); streaming normalization -14 (Spotify)
tonal balance: acoustic genres show a natural top-end decay (Pestana et al. 2013; docs/MASTERING.md)
